x: In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Commentary on Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt (Those Who Pull Forth).
The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘By those who pull forth forcefully
n
, by those who draw out gently
n

, by those who glide swiftly (3), by those who race ahead (4), and by those who manage affairs (5), on the Day the trembling one shakes (6), followed by the one that follows it (7), hearts that Day will be anxious (8), their eyes humbled (9).’ Our Lord swore by those who pull forth, and the interpreters differed about who they are and what they pull out.

Some said they are the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. Among those who held this view, ʿAbd Allāh said they are angels; Masrūq likewise identified them as angels. Ibn ʿAbbās said the phrase refers to the moment when the soul is pulled out. Ibn ʿAbbās said they pull out souls. Saʿīd said the souls are drawn out, submerged, and then cast into the Fire.
Others said it is death that pulls out souls. Mujāhid repeatedly explained it as death.
Others said they are stars that move from one horizon to another. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah identified them as stars.

Others said they are bows drawing arrows. ʿAṭāʾ said they are bows. Al-Suddī said they are souls when they are submerged in the chest. Al-Ṭabarī says the sound view is that God swore by all who pull forth forcefully; He did not specify one puller to the exclusion of another. Everything that pulls out forcefully is included in His oath, whether an angel, death, a star, a bow, or something else. The sense is pulling out completely, as an archer draws a bow to its full extent.
His saying, ‘by those who draw out gently’: the interpreters also differed over who they are and what is drawn out.

Some said they are angels who gently draw out the believer’s soul, as a knot is loosened from a camel when it is untied. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are angels. Al-Farrāʾ said he had heard Arabs say anshaṭtu and ‘as though he were loosened from a tether.’ To tie a rope around a camel’s hand is to make it nashiṭ; the one who ties it is nāshiṭ. When you bind the rope to a camel’s hand, you have tied it; when you release it, you have unbound it.
Others said it is death that releases the human soul. Mujāhid said death. Other reports from him and Ibn ʿAbbās describe the soul being drawn out or released from the feet.
Others said they are stars that move from one horizon to another; Qatādah said they are stars.

Others said they are al-awhāq, hunting nooses; ʿAṭāʾ gave this explanation. Al-Ṭabarī says the sound view is that God swore by all that moves from one place to another. He did not single out one kind. Angels move from place to place, as do death, stars, nooses, and even wild cows, as al-Ṭirimmāḥ said … … ‘Have you known anyone among the allied horsemen, other than the solitary wild cows, who was startled by them?’ He means wild cows, which travel from one region to another. Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj said, ‘Every snare’s rope has drawn it onward.’ Worries also draw a person from place to place, as Hamyān ibn Quḥāfah said: ‘My worries have set out on their courses, taking me sometimes to Syria and sometimes to Wāsiṭ.’ Everything that moves is included in the oath unless decisive evidence restricts its meaning to one kind.
His saying, ‘by those who glide swiftly’: God means those that swim or glide swiftly.
The interpreters differed about which of His creatures He swore by.

Some said it is death, which glides through the son of Adam. Mujāhid said death, though in another transmission from him it is angels descending from heaven swiftly, like a swift horse is called a swimmer when it runs fast.
Others said they are stars swimming in their orbits; Qatādah said stars.

Others said ships; ʿAṭāʾ gave that interpretation. Al-Ṭabarī says the sound view is that God swore by all His creatures that glide, without specifying one kind over another, as explained above concerning those who pull forth.
His saying, ‘by those who race ahead’: the interpreters differed.
Some said they are angels. Mujāhid said they are angels. Another report from him says they are death.
Others said they are horses that race ahead; ʿAṭāʾ said horses.
Others said they are stars, some overtaking others in their course; Qatādah said stars. Al-Ṭabarī’s view here is the same as for the preceding expressions.
His saying, ‘and those who manage affairs’: the angels who manage the matters God has commanded them to oversee.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said they are angels; another report from him gives the same explanation.

His saying, ‘on the Day the trembling one shakes’: the earth and mountains will shake at the first blast. ‘Followed by the one that follows it’ means another blast follows it, the second blast that follows the first for the raising of the dead on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbās said the trembling one is the first blast.

His saying, ‘followed by the one that follows it’: the second blast. Ibn ʿAbbās said the latter follows the former: the trembling one is the first blast and the follower is the later one. Al-Ḥasan said they are the two blasts: the first causes the living to die and the second revives the dead, citing Q 39:68. Qatādah likewise said the first blast kills everything by God’s permission and the second revives everything. The Prophet reportedly said there will be forty between them; his companions said he added nothing more. It is also related that rain called ‘life’ will fall during those forty years, the earth will become fertile and stir, and people’s bodies will grow like plants; then the second blast will be blown and they will stand looking around. A lengthy report from Abū Hurayrah describes the Trumpet as a great horn blown three times: the blast of terror, the blast that causes death, and the blast of rising.

The inhabitants of the heavens and earth will be terrified, except those God wills. God will make the blast continue without pause; it is the ‘single cry from which there is no recovery’ (Q 38:15). God will set the mountains moving and shake the earth and its inhabitants. Another report says that when the Prophet recited ‘On the Day the trembling one shakes, followed by the one that follows it,’ he said, ‘The first has come, followed by the second; death has come with all it entails.’ Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said they are the first and second blasts. Mujāhid said the earth and mountains will quake … … and that ‘the one that follows it’ refers to ‘when the heaven is split open’ (Q 84:1) and ‘the two will be crushed with one crushing’ (Q 69:14).
Others said the earth shakes and the follower is the Hour.

Ibn Zayd said the trembling one is the earth and the follower is the Hour. Arab grammarians differed about the predicate of the oath ‘By those who pull forth forcefully.’ Some Basrans said its predicate is ‘In that is a lesson for whoever fears’ (Q 79:26), or one may connect it to ‘on the Day the trembling one shakes,’ and ‘hearts that Day will be anxious.’ God’s will encompasses all of these possibilities. Some Kufans said the response to the oath is omitted because listeners know its meaning: ‘You will surely be resurrected and called to account.’ The following question, ‘Will we really be returned to our former state when we have become decayed bones?’ (Q 79:10–11) indicates this. Another Kufan said the lām cannot be omitted from the oath’s response because without it its position would be unclear. Al-Ṭabarī says the response is understood from the context and has therefore been omitted. His saying, ‘hearts that Day will be anxious’: the hearts of some of God’s creatures will be fearful of the tremendous terror that descends. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah explained it as fearful; Qatādah said they will quake from what they witness. Ibn Zayd likewise said they are afraid.

His saying, ‘their eyes humbled’: the eyes of their owners will be lowered because of the humiliation, grief, fear, and terror that overwhelm them from the great horror of that Day. Ibn Zayd said they are humbled by disgrace; Qatādah said they are abased.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘They say, “Will we really be returned to our former state (10), even after we have become decayed bones?” (11) They say, “Then that would be a losing return!” (12). It will be only one shout (13), and suddenly they will be upon the earth’s surface (14).’ God says that when these Quraysh polytheists who deny resurrection are told they will be raised after death, they say: will we return to our first state and live again as before we perished and died? The phrase ‘returned to the ḥāfirah’ is like saying someone returned to his tracks, from where he came. A poet said, ‘Would we return to baldness and gray hair? God forbid such folly and recklessness.’ Ibn ʿAbbās explained ḥāfirah as life. He also explained the verse as asking whether they will live again after death and be raised from where they are. Qatādah said it means being resurrected as a new creation. His saying, ‘even after we have become decayed bones’: they ask whether they will be returned to life after they have become worn-out bones.
His saying, ‘They say, “Then that would be a losing return!”’: if they are returned to life after becoming bones, they consider that a loss.

His saying, ‘It will be only one shout’: God will issue a single shout … … and suddenly they will be on the surface of the earth. At ‘in the original state.’ He said: that is, brought back as a new creation.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘When we have become decayed bones’: the reciters differed in its reading. Most reciters of Medina, the Hijaz, and Basra read nākhirah, ‘decayed,’ meaning worn away. Most reciters of Kufa read nākhirah with an alif, meaning hollow, with winds whistling through their cavities as they pass. Some Kufan scholars of Arabic said that nākhirah and nakhirah mean the same, like ṭāmiʿ and ṭamiʿ (‘covetous’) or bākhal and bakhil (‘miserly’). The more eloquent and better-known of the two forms to us is nakhirah, without an alif, meaning decayed. Yet the verse endings before and after it have an alif, so I would prefer adding one here to make it match the other verse endings; absent that consideration, the reading without the alif would be more preferable to me.
Among those who said nakhirah means decayed was Ibn ʿAbbas:

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And suddenly they are upon the surface’: God, exalted is His mention, says that these deniers of resurrection, who wondered at God bringing them back to life after death, will suddenly be upon the surface of the earth. The Arabs call the open wilderness and the earth’s surface sāhirah. It seems they gave it this name because animals sleep and keep vigil there, naming the place after what occurs upon it. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Ṣalt said: ‘On it is the game of the plain and of the sea…’ He also said, as related by the brother of Nahm on the day of Dhu Qar to his horse: ‘Charge, Muḥāj! x: Regarding His saying, ‘Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed’: God, exalted is His mention, says that Moses’ Lord called to him, telling him to go to Pharaoh. The particle ‘that’ is omitted, since the call was speech; it is as though He said to Moses: ‘Go to Pharaoh.’
Regarding His saying, ‘He has transgressed’: that is, he has grown arrogant and exceeded all bounds in aggression and pride toward his Lord.
Regarding His saying, ‘And say: Would you purify yourself?’ He says: Tell him, ‘Would you be willing to cleanse yourself of the filth of unbelief and believe in your Lord?’

Abū ʿAmr was reported to read it with a doubled zāy, taking it to mean giving alms, from tatazakkā with assimilation. But Moses was not calling Pharaoh, an unbeliever, to give charity; he was calling him to Islam. Thus tazakkā means ‘become pure,’ that is, become a believing Muslim. The light zāy is the more eloquent of the two readings in Arabic.

Regarding His saying, ‘Then he showed him the great sign’: God says that Moses showed Pharaoh the great sign, the greatest proof that God had sent him as a messenger. That sign was Moses’ hand when he drew it out white before those looking on, and his staff when it became a manifest serpent.

x: Regarding ‘I am your highest lord,’ he said: those are the two statements for which God seized him as a chastisement for the latter and the former. He was asked, ‘Who told you this?’ He replied, ‘Abu Ḥuṣayn.’ He was asked, ‘From Abu al-Ḍuḥā, from Ibn ʿAbbās?’ He said, ‘Yes.’

c: Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, from his father, from his uncle, from his father, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘So God seized him in punishment for the latter and the former’: the former was when he said, ‘I know of no god for you other than myself’; the latter was when he said, ‘I am your highest lord.’

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Waḍḍāḥ, from ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Jazarī, from Mujāhid, who said
m: concerning the verse… …that it refers to his statement, ‘I know of no god for you other than myself,’ and his statement, ‘I am your highest lord.’ Forty years separated them.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Abū ʿAwānah, from Ismāʿīl al-Asadī, from al-Shaʿbī,
m: with the same account.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Zakariyyā, from ʿĀmir, who said
m: ‘the latter and the former’ are his two statements: ‘I know of no god for you other than myself’ and ‘I am your highest lord.’

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: the former was ‘I know of no god for you other than myself,’ and the latter was ‘I am your highest lord.’

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, who said
m: he heard Mujāhid say that forty years passed between Pharaoh’s two statements.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us, saying he heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say: the former was when Pharaoh said, ‘I know of no god for you other than myself,’ and the latter when he said, ‘I am your highest lord.’ God seized him for both statements and drowned him in the sea.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying that people differed over this: some said the ‘latter and former’ refer to Pharaoh’s two statements, ‘I know of no god for you other than myself’ and ‘I am your highest lord.’

x: Others said it means the punishment of this world and the punishment of the next: God hastened his drowning while reserving punishment for him in the Hereafter.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Khaythamah al-Juʿfī, who said
m: forty years separated Pharaoh’s two statements.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Isrāʾīl, from Thuwair, from Mujāhid, who said
m: Pharaoh remained among his people for forty years after saying, ‘I am your highest lord.’

x: Others said that God seized him as a chastisement in this world and the next.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from Hawdhah, from ʿAwf, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: it means this world and the next.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: it means the punishment of this world and the next. This was also Qatādah’s view.

x: Others said the ‘former’ was his disobedience and disbelief in his Lord, while the ‘latter’ was… Others said that the former refers to Pharaoh’s disobedience and disbelief in his Lord, while the latter is his statement, ‘I am your highest lord.’

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Ismāʿīl ibn Sumayʿ, from Abū Razīn,
m: concerning the verse: the former was his denial and disobedience; the latter was his saying, ‘I am your highest lord.’

x: ‘He denied and disobeyed; then he turned away, striving; he gathered and proclaimed; and said, “I am your highest lord.”’
That was his final statement.
Others said that the meaning is that God seized him for his first and last deeds.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid,
m: who explained the verse as referring to Pharaoh’s first and last deed.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid,
m: with the same explanation: his first and last actions.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from al-Kalbī, who said
m: the latter and former chastisement refers to Pharaoh’s disobedience and what preceded it.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Jarīr, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning ‘the latter and the former’: his deeds in the latter and former periods. Regarding His saying, ‘Surely in that is a lesson for whoever fears’: God says that the punishment He inflicted on Pharaoh in this world, and His seizing him as a chastisement for the latter and the former, provide an admonition and lesson for whoever fears God and His punishment. The word nakāl (‘chastisement’) is expressed as a verbal noun after ‘God seized him’ because the sense is ‘God made an example of him’; thus nakāl is derived from the meaning, not the wording, of ‘He seized him.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Are you harder to create, or the heaven? He built it’: God addresses the Quraysh who denied resurrection and said, ‘When we have become decayed bones, will we then be brought back?’ He says: Are you people harder to create, or the heaven your Lord built? The One who built the heaven and raised it as a canopy can easily create you and those like you and bring you to life after death. Creating you after death is no harder than creating the heaven. ‘He built it’ means He raised it and made it a roof over the earth.
Regarding His saying, ‘He raised its vault and proportioned it’: God says that He made the heaven even, with no part higher or lower than another, but all of it level in height and extension.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning ‘He raised its vault and proportioned it’: He raised its structure and made it even.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: of ‘He raised its vault’: He raised its structure without pillars.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: who explained it as ‘its structure.’ Commentary on God’s saying: ‘He darkened its night and brought forth its brightness; and after that He spread out the earth. He brought forth from it its water and pasture, and set the mountains firmly.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘He darkened its night’: God says that He made the heaven’s night dark. He attributed the night to the heaven because the sun’s setting and rising occur in it; it is attributed to it for that reason, just as one says ‘the stars of the night’ because they rise and set in it.

Regarding His saying, ‘He darkened its night’: God says He made the heaven’s night dark. He attributed the night to the heaven because the sun’s setting and rising occur in it; it is attributed to it since those events take place there, just as one says ‘the stars of the night’ because they rise and set in it.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘He darkened its night’: He made its night dark.

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, through his father and uncle, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: it means ‘He made it dark.’

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: likewise.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd’s explanation as ‘the darkness.’

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say that ʿUbayd related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk… …who explained ‘He darkened its night’ as ‘He made its night dark.’

c: Muḥammad ibn Sinān al-Qazzāz related to us, from Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar, from al-Ḥakam, from ʿIkrimah,
m: who gave the same explanation.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And brought forth its brightness’: He brought forth its light, meaning that He brought out and made manifest its daytime and illuminated its morning.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid,
m: who explained it as ‘He illuminated it.’

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said
m: He illuminated its light.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say that ʿUbayd reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk… …who said it means its daylight.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd’s explanation of ‘its brightness’ as ‘the light of daytime.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And after that He spread out the earth’: the interpreters differed over ‘after that.’
Some said the earth was spread out after the heaven was created.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: explaining that although God mentioned the earth’s creation before the heaven and then mentioned the heaven before the earth, He created the earth and its provisions without spreading it out before creating the heaven. He then turned to the heaven and made it seven heavens, and afterward spread out the earth. This is the meaning of ‘And after that He spread out the earth.’

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, through his father and uncle, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning these verses: God created the heavens and earth; when He finished the heavens, before bringing forth the earth’s provisions, He placed those provisions in it after the heaven had been created and firmly set the mountains—meaning that He spread it out. The earth’s provisions and growth would not be fit without night and day. That is the meaning of ‘And after that He spread out the earth.’ Have you not heard Him say, ‘He brought forth from it its water and pasture’?

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Yaʿqūb, from Ḥafṣ, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: that God placed the House upon water, on four foundations, two thousand years before creating the world; then the earth was spread from beneath the House.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Bukayr ibn al-Akhnas, from Mujāhid, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, who said
m: that God created the House two thousand years before the earth, and the earth was spread from it.

x: Others said that the sense is ‘and He spread out the earth along with that.’ They said that the earth was created and spread out before the heaven, since God says, ‘It is He who created for you all that is on earth, then turned to the heaven and fashioned it into seven heavens’
r
. They argued that God thus reports fashioning the heavens after creating all that is on earth. If so, they said, ‘And after that He spread out the earth’ can only mean what they have stated:
He spread it out along with that. They cited ‘a coarse fellow, and after that a bastard’
meaning ‘along with that a bastard’; the saying to a man, ‘You are foolish, and after that of ignoble lineage,’ meaning ‘along with that’; and ‘We wrote in the Psalms after the Reminder’
r
, meaning before the Reminder. They also cited a Hudhayl poem: ‘I praised my God after ʿUrwah had escaped—Khirāsh escaped too, and some evil is less than other evil.’
They claimed Khirāsh escaped before ʿUrwah.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Sufyān, from Khuṣayf, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning ‘And after that He spread out the earth’: ‘along with that He spread it out.’

c: Ibn Bashshār related to me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Mujāhid,
m: who read it ‘And the earth, at that time, He spread out.’

c: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam related to us, from ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad, from Muḥammad ibn Salamah, from Khuṣayf, from Mujāhid,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Muḥammad ibn Khalaf al-ʿAsqalānī related to me, from Rawwād ibn al-Jarrāḥ, from Abū Ḥamzah, from al-Suddī,
m: who also said ‘along with that He spread it out.’ The view we related from Ibn ʿAbbās—that God created the earth and determined its provisions without spreading it out, then fashioned the seven heavens, and afterward spread the earth, bringing forth its water and pasture and setting its mountains firmly—better accords with the apparent wording of revelation. God says ‘after that,’ whose familiar meaning is the opposite of ‘before.’ God’s spreading the earth after fashioning the seven heavens, darkening its night, and bringing forth its brightness does not require that the earth itself was created after the heavens. Spreading means stretching out and extending in Arabic: daḥā yadḥū daḥwan and daḥā yadḥī daḥyan are two forms… …Among the poetry is Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s saying: ‘A dwelling He spread out, then let us inhabit; and He stayed in the other, the more exalted.’ And Aws ibn Ḥajar said in describing rain: ‘It drives pebbles from the earth’s surface, surging—as though it were one searching or playing at daḥw.’ Most interpreters held the meaning of ‘He spread it out’ to be as we have explained.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said
m: it means ‘He spread it out.’

c: Muḥammad ibn Khalaf related to me, from Rawwād, from Abū Ḥamzah, from al-Suddī,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān,
m: who likewise said ‘He spread it out.’ Ibn Zayd gave a different explanation:

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported him as saying that it means He plowed it and split it open. He recited ‘Then We split the earth open’ through ‘and fruit and fodder’
r
, explaining that when He split it, He made these things grow from it. He also recited ‘By the earth that cracks open’
r
. Regarding His saying, ‘He brought forth from it its water’: He made rivers flow in it. ‘And its pasture’ means He caused its vegetation to grow.

x: The interpreters said similarly.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say that ʿUbayd reported hearing al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain ‘its pasture’ as all the plants God created in it, and ‘its water’ as the rivers He made flow there.

evidence.text: Ibn Bashshār related to me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Mujāhid, who read it ‘And the earth, at that time, He spread out.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And the mountains He set firmly’: He fixed the mountains in the earth. The words omit ‘in it,’ which is understood from the context; the meaning is ‘He set the mountains firmly in it.’

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning ‘He set them firmly’: He fixed them so the earth would not sway with its inhabitants.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Jarīr, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, from ʿAlī, who said:
m: When God created the earth, it convulsed and said, ‘Will You create Adam and his descendants upon me, and they will cast their filth upon me and commit sins upon me?’ So God anchored it. Some of its mountains you see, and some you do not…

x: …and the earth’s first firming was like the flesh of a slaughtered camel, with its meat quivering. …some of which you see and some of which you do not. The earth’s first stabilization was like the flesh of a slaughtered camel, its meat quivering.

Commentary on God’s saying: ‘As provision for you and your livestock. Then, when the Great Overwhelming Event comes, the day a person remembers what he strove for and Hell is exposed to whoever sees it.’ By ‘as provision for you and your livestock,’ God means that He created these things and brought forth the earth’s water and pasture for our benefit and enjoyment for a time.

Regarding His saying, ‘Then, when the Great Overwhelming Event comes’: that is, when the event that overwhelms every terrifying occurrence arrives, engulfing all else with its tremendous terror. It is also said that this is one of the names of the Resurrection.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘when the Great Overwhelming Event comes’: it is one of the names of the Resurrection; God magnified it and warned His servants of it.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿUmārah related to me, from Sahl ibn ʿĀmir, from Mālik ibn Mighwal, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Walīd, who said
m: concerning the verse: the people of Paradise will be led to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘The day a person remembers what he strove for’: when the Overwhelming Event comes, a person will remember… …what he did in this world, both good and evil; that is his striving. ‘And Hell is exposed’: it is brought forth and displayed—God’s Fire—to whoever sees it, that is, to the eyes of those looking on.

Commentary on God’s saying: ‘As for him who transgressed and preferred the life of this world, Hell will be his refuge. But as for him who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from desire, Paradise will be his refuge.’ God, exalted is His mention, says: As for the one who defied his Lord, disobeyed Him, and was too proud to worship Him.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid,
m: who explained ‘transgressed’ as ‘disobeyed.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘and preferred the life of this world’: he chose this world’s enjoyments over the honor of the Hereafter and what God has prepared there for His beloved servants. He worked and strove for this world and left aside work for the Hereafter. ‘Hell will be his refuge’: God’s Fire, whose name is Hell, will be his dwelling and refuge, the destination to which he will go on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding His saying, ‘But as for him who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from desire’: he feared that God would question him when he stood before Him on the Day of Resurrection, and so he was mindful of Him by fulfilling His obligations and avoiding disobedience. ‘And restrained his soul from desire’ means he held it back from what God dislikes and does not approve of, curbing it and opposing its desires in favor of what his Lord commanded. ‘Paradise will be his refuge’: Paradise will be his abode and dwelling on the Day of Resurrection. We have already mentioned the interpreters’ views on the meaning of ‘for whoever fears standing before his Lord’
r
, which makes it unnecessary to repeat them here.

Commentary on God’s saying: ‘They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? What have you to do with mentioning it? Its ultimate knowledge belongs to your Lord. You are only a warner to those who fear it. On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained only an evening or its morning.’ God says to His Prophet Muḥammad: These deniers of resurrection ask you about the Hour, when the dead will be raised from their graves: ‘When will it be established and appear?’ Al-Farrāʾ used to say: If someone asks why the Hour is described as being ‘anchored,’ when anchoring applies to ships and firmly rooted mountains, I would answer that it is like a ship underway that then comes to rest: its anchoring is its standing. Its standing is not like a person standing; it is like the expressions ‘justice has stood’ or ‘the truth has stood,’ meaning it has appeared and become established.

Abū Jaʿfar says: God’s words ‘What have you to do with mentioning it?’ mean: What business have you with discussing the Hour and investigating its affair? It is reported that the Messenger of God did not often mention the Hour until this verse was revealed.

c: Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm related to me, from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah, who said:
m: The Prophet continued to be asked about the Hour until God revealed, ‘What have you to do with mentioning it? Its ultimate knowledge belongs to your Lord.’

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Ismāʿīl, from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, who said
m: that the Prophet kept speaking about the Hour until ‘They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?’ through ‘those who fear it’ was revealed.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid,
m: who explained ‘What have you to do with mentioning it?’ as referring to the Hour.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Its ultimate knowledge belongs to your Lord’: the limit of its knowledge is with your Lord; that is, knowledge of when the Hour will occur ends with Him alone. No one else knows its appointed time.

Regarding His saying, ‘You are only a warner to those who fear it’: God says to Muḥammad that he is only a messenger sent to warn of the Hour those who fear God’s punishment for their sins on that day. He was not charged with knowing when it would occur. He says: Leave what you were not charged to know, and do what you were commanded—warn those you were commanded to warn. The reciters differed in reading ‘a warner to whoever fears it.’ Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Muḥayṣin read mundhirun, with tanwīn, meaning ‘a warner to whoever fears it.’ The other reciters of Medina, Mecca, Kufa, and Basra read mundhiru man, with ‘warner’ in a construct phrase with ‘whoever.’ The soundest view in my judgment is that both are established readings, and whichever one a reciter uses is correct.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in reading ‘a warner to whoever fears it.’
The other reciters of Medina, Mecca, Kufa, and Basra read mundhiru man, with ‘warner’ in a construct phrase with ‘whoever.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had remained only an evening or its morning’: God says that when these deniers of the Hour see that it has arrived, in view of its tremendous terror, it will seem as though they had remained in this world for only the evening of a day or the morning of that same day. The Arabs say, ‘I will come to you in the evening or its morning,’ and ‘I will come in the morning or its evening,’ using ‘morning’ for the start of the day and ‘evening’ for its end. Thus ‘only an evening or its morning’ means only the end or beginning of a day. The following verse is cited: ‘We came upon ʿĀmir at her dwelling in the evening of the crescent moon, or its last night’—that is, the evening of the crescent, or the evening when it had nearly disappeared.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning the verse: The duration of this world will seem brief to them when they witness the Hereafter. This concludes the commentary on Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt.
